method: The modified EUI-64 rule builds a 64-bit interface identifier from an individual (unicast) MAC address or EUI-64 identifier. For a 48-bit MAC the universal/local (U/L) bit in the first octet, bit 1 with mask 0x02, is flipped, and FF FE is inserted between the first three bytes (the OUI) and the last three bytes, producing eight bytes. A 64-bit EUI-64 input only has its U/L bit flipped; FF FE is not inserted a second time. An odd first octet has the I/G (multicast) bit set, so the tool rejects it instead of generating an identifier from a group address. The link-local address is fe80::/64 followed by the identifier; a global or unique-local address is the selected /64 prefix followed by the identifier, with any bits beyond the 64th cleared. The identifier is shown as four 4-digit lowercase hex groups, and addresses use the RFC 5952 canonical text form: lowercase, no leading zeros, and the longest run (the first on a tie) of two or more zero groups collapsed to ::. The tool requires a /64 prefix because the identifier is exactly 64 bits, and everything is computed in the page with no uploads, network requests or storage.

sources.title: RFC 4291 section 2.5.1: an EUI-64 interface identifier flips the universal/local bit, and a 48-bit MAC gets FF FE inserted in the middle.
RFC 4291 section 2.5.3: the link-local address is formed from the fe80::/64 prefix and the interface identifier.
RFC 5952 section 4: IPv6 text representation uses lowercase hex, no leading zeros, and :: for the longest run of zero groups, the first run on a tie.
RFC 4862 section 5.3: stateless address autoconfiguration combines a /64 prefix with an interface identifier of the same length.
